claim: NPVF and the hypothalamic neurons that produce it are a sleep-promoting system.
source: We previously identified neuropeptide VF (NPVF) and the hypothalamic neurons that produce it as a sleep-promoting system (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2017

claim: npvf-expressing neurons control sleep via the serotonergic raphe nuclei (RN).
source: Here we show using zebrafish that npvf-expressing neurons control sleep via the serotonergic raphe nuclei (RN), a hindbrain structure that is critical for sleep in both diurnal zebrafish and nocturnal mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including genetic labeling, calcium imaging, chemogenetic and optogenetic experiments

claim: The serotonergic raphe nuclei are critical for sleep in both diurnal zebrafish and nocturnal mice.
source: Here we show using zebrafish that npvf-expressing neurons control sleep via the serotonergic raphe nuclei (RN), a hindbrain structure that is critical for sleep in both diurnal zebrafish and nocturnal mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: npvf-expressing neurons innervate serotonergic RN neurons.
source: Using genetic labeling and calcium imaging, we show that npvf-expressing neurons innervate and can activate serotonergic RN neurons.
evidence: Supported by genetic labeling data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: npvf-expressing neurons can activate serotonergic RN neurons.
source: Using genetic labeling and calcium imaging, we show that npvf-expressing neurons innervate and can activate serotonergic RN neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires NPVF.
source: We also demonstrate that chemogenetic or optogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires NPVF and serotonin in the RN.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic stimulation data in npvf mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires NPVF.
source: We also demonstrate that chemogenetic or optogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires NPVF and serotonin in the RN.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation data in npvf mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires serotonin in the RN.
source: We also demonstrate that chemogenetic or optogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires NPVF and serotonin in the RN.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic stimulation data in tph2 mutants and RN-ablated animals shown in Figures 4 and 6

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires serotonin in the RN.
source: We also demonstrate that chemogenetic or optogenetic stimulation of npvf-expressing neurons induces sleep in a manner that requires NPVF and serotonin in the RN.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation data in tph2 mutants and RN-ablated animals shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: NPVF acts upstream of serotonin in the RN to maintain normal sleep levels.
source: Finally, we provide genetic evidence that NPVF acts upstream of serotonin in the RN to maintain normal sleep levels.
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 3

claim: The serotonergic raphe nuclei are critical for the initiation and maintenance of sleep in zebrafish and mice.
source: Recent evidence from zebrafish and mice demonstrate that the serotonergic raphe nuclei (RN) are critical for the initiation and maintenance of sleep (Iwasaki et al., 2018; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Venner et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2018), in contrast with previous models suggesting a wake-promoting role for the RN that were largely based on their wake-active nature (Saper and Fuller, 2017; Scammell et al., 2017; Weber and Dan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Previous models suggested a wake-promoting role for the RN based on their wake-active nature.
source: Recent evidence from zebrafish and mice demonstrate that the serotonergic raphe nuclei (RN) are critical for the initiation and maintenance of sleep (Iwasaki et al., 2018; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Venner et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2018), in contrast with previous models suggesting a wake-promoting role for the RN that were largely based on their wake-active nature (Saper and Fuller, 2017; Scammell et al., 2017; Weber and Dan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Mutation of tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (tph2) in zebrafish results in reduced sleep.
source: In zebrafish, mutation of tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (tph2), which is required for serotonin (5-HT) synthesis in the RN, results in reduced sleep, sleep depth, and homeostatic response to sleep deprivation (Oikonomou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oikonomou et al., 2019

claim: Mutation of tph2 in zebrafish results in reduced sleep depth.
source: In zebrafish, mutation of tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (tph2), which is required for serotonin (5-HT) synthesis in the RN, results in reduced sleep, sleep depth, and homeostatic response to sleep deprivation (Oikonomou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oikonomou et al., 2019

claim: The gradual return to baseline of GCaMP6s fluorescence is consistent with the prolonged effect expected for neuropeptide/GPCR signaling.
